title: 196 deadlocks to zero
subtitle: Measuring a write path from the database itself, and finding that one index was the whole problem

lede: A bulk update workload through my shared write path had slowed to a crawl, with deadlocks every few seconds. The queue in front of the database reported healthy throughput, which was the first clue that the queue was the wrong instrument. I built a harness that measured from the only place that knows how many rows were committed, the database itself, and compared runs before and after a single schema change. The write path is shared by every producer in the estate, so a slow write path slows everything. The obvious metrics were the queue's own counters, and they measure intake: how much work was taken in, and nothing about how much landed.
quote: Only the database knows how many rows were committed.
evidence: PostgreSQL performance tuning: a unique index on the update key took deadlocks during a bulk update from 196 to 0 on a write path shared by every producer.
Performance benchmarking methodology: a harness that samples system load, queue depth and PostgreSQL tuple deltas and compares runs before and after one change, measuring committed rows, not intake.
Write-path throughput: 1.25 M rows committed in 185 seconds after the fix, 16,370 a second at peak and 6,752 on average.
Latency diagnosis: batch latency from 100 to 2,000 ms before the index and 7 to 37 ms after it.
author: Corey James
